Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today for this critical event, Protecting Children in Armed Conflict from Explosive Weapons in an Era of Evolving Warfare. I'm Laura Miller. I'm the CEO of the War Child Alliance. And we together are here for one reason. Children are being killed, maimed, traumatized by explosive weapons. This harm has been rising for a decade, but in the last few years, it has not simply increased, it has surged. Meanwhile, the very institutions meant to protect children are failing them. The latest UN Secretary-General's report on children in armed conflict shows that last year, states were the primary perpetrators of grave violations against children. This should be unacceptable to everyone in this room. We are meeting here on the margins of the UN General Assembly, with the world's decision makers gathered in one place. That is a privileged position, and it comes with a responsibility. We have representatives of states, NGOs, international organizations. Between us, we hold political power, legal expertise, the operational reach, and the moral authority to change this. Before we begin our main discussion on the devastating impacts of explosive weapons on children, I would like to invite everyone to join me in a moment of silence. Please remain seated, and let us take time to honour the countless children killed, those who carry physical and psychological injuries, and the families and communities carrying the pain of violence and conflict. Thank you. As we begin today's discussion, my hope is that through this event, we move beyond discussion to urgent action. And we have exceptional speakers and panelists here to help move this agenda forward. To begin, I am very pleased to introduce Malta's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Chris Fearn, to share opening remarks. Malta has been a steadfast champion of children affected by conflict, and it is my great pleasure to hand the floor to Minister Fearn.

Thank you and good morning. I want you to picture, if you can, a rocket-propelled grenade launcher, RPGs. Some of you might have seen them in action. But you've all seen pictures of these. They're like these big bazookas with a large grenade. They're usually used to stop tanks or to down helicopters. Just keep that image in your mind. Before I went into politics, I spent 25 years as a pediatric surgeon doing operations on children. And one sunny morning, about 12 years ago, got a phone call from somebody in Tripoli, in Libya, about just 100 kilometers, 150 kilometers away from Malta, saying, "We have a six-year-old girl who's been hit by a rocket-propelled grenade. There is an air ambulance which happens to be in Tripoli, it came over for something else. We're going to put her on the spray and send her to you. And we said, yes, yes, we'll have her. And literally within an hour and a half, we had this beautiful six-year-old girl with a ponytail, her abdomen wrapped in bandages, and we went straight to the operating theatre. And when we took off the bandages, there was a gaping hole in her abdomen. And over the next two days, I spent 18, 19 hours taking out bits of her bowels, which had been destroyed, and recreating her abdominal wall. The operation went well. But the blast, the shockwave of the explosion, had literally melted this girl's lungs. And over the next three or four days, despite being in intensive care, despite being ventilated and intubated, her condition deteriorated, and on the sixth day, she died. Her name was Fatima. That's one girl with one family. Last year alone, the United Nations registered, there must be much more than this, but registered 14,200 girls and boys who are casualties of war. 14,200 little Fatimas. It is within our power to stop this. Wars are not natural disasters. They are man-made disasters. They are started by men. They are conducted by men. They can be prevented and stopped by men and women. If you haven't signed the political declaration on explosive weapons in populated areas, please do so. Thank you.

Thank you, Minister Fern, for your reflections and for your continued leadership and for setting the stage for our discussion today. I'd now like to introduce our panelists. We have Mr. Mohamed Yakhya, Assistant Secretary General for Humanitarian Affairs and Deputy Emergency Relief Coordinator. Mr. Olof Skoug, Deputy Secretary General for Political Affairs of the European External Action Service. Ms. Hanan Suleiman, UNICEF Deputy Executive Director, and Mr. Marcus Mumford, War Child Alliance Founding Global Ambassador. Thank you all for being here. I'd like to start with a question to you, Mr. Yahya. OCHA plays a central role in advancing the protection of civilians, including tracking, analyzing, and regularly reporting on protection of civilians across conflicts worldwide. Can you share with us what you, OCHA, are seeing in terms of the impact of explosive weapons on civilians? And what should states and parties to conflict do to control their escalating use?

Thank you very much. Thank you for having us, and thank you to Malta, Norway, and World Child for sponsoring this event. From our perspective, what we are seeing I think was aptly described by the Foreign Minister, across different areas from Congo or countries such as Congo to Lebanon, to Myanmar, to Sudan, to Ukraine, to occupied Palestinian territories, civilians are being killed and maimed in their homes, in their communities. Drones are increasingly carrying explosive weapons into populated areas, bringing battlefield closer to people's homes, schools, and communities. And you see them everywhere, especially how drones have changed the conflict, but also how it has changed and impacted civilians. Children are among those who are paying the highest price. Single explosion can change everything. A parent killed, a child loses a limb, a family loses home. But harm goes beyond those killed or injured. You destroy a hospital, healthcare disappears. You destroy a water system, and disease spreads. You destroy a school, and children lose not only education, but a place of safety and normality. Humanitarian access becomes very difficult. Aid workers are being pushed back from the front line, and you probably know, last year we lost about 1,000 aid workers across these battlefields. But schools and learning places are also being destroyed. When healthcare is damaged, treatment disappears, people die from preventable diseases, and danger can remain long after the fighting ends. Explosive remnants, contaminated homes, streets, farmlands, playgrounds prevent families from returning home and rebuilding their communities. We know this. We know the consequences of explosive weapons. They're documented. They're foreseeable. What makes this tragedy even more unacceptable is that it's preventable. It's man-made. It's choices we make. That's why the Secretary-General has repeatedly called for parties in conflict to avoid the use of explosive weapons in populated areas. And that's why states and parties to conflict must take meaningful steps to change the ways military operations are conducted in towns and in cities. The tools already exist. States have adopted the political declaration on explosive weapons in populated areas. Now we need action. We need more states, as the foreign minister called on, to endorse the declaration. We need those commitments translated into military policy, planning, and practice. We want to see parties avoid the use of explosive weapons in wider effect in populated areas. Arms transfers must not contribute to patterns of harm to civilians. As drones and other technologies change how wars are fought, innovation must be used to minimize civilian harm and not multiply it. But ultimately, the implementation is measured not in policy papers, but in lives saved. I hope this discussion we have today brings us closer to action, especially for Member States. Last week, just to say, this week, it seems like last week, I've run out of how many meetings we've been in. Let me just say, a few days ago, what is becoming really interesting in this, when we talk about conflicts and harm, is that states are playing a disproportionate role in bringing these harms. It's not non-state actors, it's the state actors, which makes this issue even more urgent. Many of those states come to this General Assembly. So the power is here, it's with member states to make sure this is stopped. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Mr. Yahya, for bringing that emphasis on the role and responsibility of state actors. And now I'm pleased to bring in UNICEF's Deputy Executive Director, Ms. Suliman. She has been a leader in advocating against the use of explosive weapons and its devastating impact on children. What trends is UNICEF seeing when it comes to the impact of explosive weapons on children? How is UNICEF responding to address this impact? and what is required from partners?

Thank you very much. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, let me begin by thanking the Minister of Foreign Affairs from Malta and the organizers for bringing urgent attention to this issue. I want to begin with the painful truth that children living through armed conflict know all too well. Explosive weapons in populated areas are by far the leading cause of children being killed or maimed in conflict. United Nations verified data presented in the Secretary General's 2026 annual report on children and armed conflict shows that 72% of verified cases of children killed or maimed were caused by explosive weapons, including heavy bombs, artillery shells, grenades, missiles, landmines, and improvised explosive devices. Aerial operations, including armed drones, have been the leading cause of child casualties, accounting for almost 30% of verified killing and maiming over the past five years. They have also been responsible for the killing and maiming of humanitarian personnel, including our own in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March this year. The danger does not end when the fighting stops. Unexploded ordnance continue to kill and maim for years. Every shell left in a field, schoolyard, or alley is a death sentence waiting to be triggered. The trend is worsening. In 2025, the proportion of children killed or maimed by explosive weapons was 25% higher than in 2021. That is a staggering increase. Behind every statistic is a child whose life has been shattered. Consider 11-year-old Ibrahim in Tawila, my home country of Sudan. While fleeing Al-Fashir, he stopped to rest by the roadside, just to rest, when a shell landed beside him. The shrapnel tore into his legs and killed his brother. Ibrahim had to leave his brother behind as he fled in search of medical care. When our teams last spoke with him, he was still waiting for surgery and living with profound trauma. For every child killed, many more are injured, often with lifelong disabilities. Survivors may lose their sight, hearing, limbs, or ability to speak. Their prospects for survival and recovery are often worse than those of adults, especially when lifesaving, age-appropriate services are unavailable. The harm is also psychological. Repeated blasts generate fear, anxiety, and helplessness, and children must cope with long and difficult recovery processes. When explosive weapons kill parents and caregivers, children lose the very support networks they need to recover physically and emotionally. The effects reverberate far beyond the blast site. Explosive weapons in populated areas destroy the infrastructure that children depend on: water and sanitation systems, power networks, health facilities, and schools. It disrupts learning, blocks humanitarian supplies, prevents food and essential services from reaching the most vulnerable families. Ibrahim's story and the worsening global trend must compel urgent action. Preventing the use of explosive weapons in populated areas is one of the clearest steps we can take to protect children and prevent casualties before they occur. Let me therefore make three urgent calls to action. First, change the conduct of hostilities. All parties to conflict must respect international humanitarian law and uphold children's rights, including by avoiding the use of explosive weapons in populated areas. Those responsible for unlawful harm must be held accountable, and child victims must have access to effective remedies. Second, turn political commitments into practical action. All member states should endorse the political declaration. The 91 states that have already shown leadership and done so should now accelerate implementation, including through civilian protection policies with specific measures to reduce harm to children. States supplying weapons must halt transfers wherever there is a clear risk that those weapons will be used to commit grave violations against children, which we have seen in many countries. Third, meet children's immediate and long-term needs. UNICEF and our humanitarian partners provide life-saving assistance to survivors, including medical care, assistive devices such as prosthetic limbs, cash support, education, and mental health and psychosocial support. With our partners, we rehabilitate damaged water and sanitation systems, and we strengthen national and local capacity to protect and support children with disabilities. To sustain this work, we need safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access, and protection must be prioritized in humanitarian response plans, and funding decisions are needed. But assistance, however vital, cannot prevent the initial harm. As the minister said, the best protection is prevention. We must prevent the use of explosive weapons, especially in densely populated areas where children live, learn, and seek care. Excellencies, protecting children from these weapons must be a collective priority. We know the harm. We know how to reduce it. What is needed is political will to act. The cost of inaction is measured in the number of children that are killed, injured, and permanently scarred day after day. We urge you to move beyond commitment and to use every tool available to ensure that no child pays that price. Thank you.

Thank you, Ms. Suleiman, for those clear recommendations for action. Now I'm pleased to bring in Mr. Skoug from the EU. Mr. Skoug, the EU has taken a strong approach to institutionalize the children in armed conflict agenda and has included this as a top priority within the EU strategic approach to humanitarian diplomacy. What steps is the EU taking in practice to make the protection of children in conflict a priority to foreign policy and humanitarian diplomacy? And what lessons can other regional systems take away?

Good morning, everyone. Thank you, moderator, Minister, my dear friend Vanessa, Excellencies, and friends around the table here in this hall. Thank you very much for the invitation. The years after the establishment of the children and armed conflict mandate, we should be able to say that children are safer from war. Unfortunately, as we know, the opposite is true. The latest Secretary General's report records the highest number of children affected by armed conflicts since the children and armed conflict mandate was established. Killing and maiming of children is now the most prevalent grave violation, and more than 70% of child casualties are caused by explosive weapons. So thank you again for organizing us today and see what we can do to change that trend. Because it's true, as many have said, that these figures must now translate into action. For us, and thank you for the question, the protection of children affected by armed conflict is a core priority. We have reviewed our internal guidelines on children and armed conflict, and we're putting prevention, protection, and accountability at the heart of that engagement. We act through our dialogues with governments, our security and defense missions around the world, and our partnerships with the United Nations, in particular, other regional organizations and civil society, of course. The devastating impact of explosive weapons in populated areas makes respect for international humanitarian law more important than ever. Schools and hospitals must be protected. Humanitarian access must be ensured. And political commitments, including the declaration on explosive weapons in populated areas, must now translate into concrete changes in policy and in military practice. This is also at the heart of our renewed approach to humanitarian action. The new vision that we are looking to implement, and it was presented jointly by the European Commission and the High Representative Kaja Kallas in May, and it's built around three pillars: protect, perform and partner. Under PROTECT, we are stepping up humanitarian diplomacy to defend international humanitarian law, secure humanitarian access, and prevent grave violations against children, a key priority of this strategic approach, as I mentioned. Importantly, protecting children can also create openings for peace. Even in deeply polarized conflicts, their access to healthcare, nutrition, education, and safety can provide, and it should provide, common ground for humanitarian negotiations, local protection arrangements, and de-escalation that could lead also to sustainable peace agreements. And protection cannot end when the fighting dies down. Children face displacement, disrupted education, and profound mental health and psychosocial consequences long after an attack. Children with disabilities face additional barriers to accessing essential services and require particular attention. Finally, we must listen to children themselves. Child participation is a central principle of our policy. Children affected by conflict must have a meaningful voice in decisions that concern them. And as we mark now the 30 years of the mandate of the children and armed conflict, our task is not simply to reaffirm existing commitments, it's really to implement them. to defend international law and ensure accountability when it is violated. So just to reaffirm again that we remain very, very committed to this agenda and to working with all of you to turn these commitments and greater protection for children on the ground. I just want to end on a personal note. I served many years in the UN, including as the chair of the working group in the Security Council for the children in armed conflict. It's true that since then, geopolitical tensions have increased. The Security Council is often blocked in terms of hindering the UN to do its work in many of these areas. But it's amazing, and I think it's an accountability issue for every member of the Security Council to at least ensure agreement on what has to be the obvious protection of children in all of these situations. I thank you very much.

Thank you, Mr. Skou, for your personal note and also for emphasizing that an investment in children is an investment in peace. I'd like now to turn to our final panelist today. Marcus Mumford is one of War Child's founding global ambassadors. Marcus, you've been a longstanding advocate for children, and you've traveled to many countries where you've seen the impacts of conflict firsthand. We were just in Lebanon together a few weeks ago. Can you share with us a bit about what you've seen specifically in terms of the psychological impacts of war on children? And what would be your message to member states and institutions with the ability to influence the extent to which children are protected?

Thank you. Protection of children is surely the clearest measurement of our shared humanity. By that measure, something is catastrophically wrong. I've been an ambassador for the War Child Alliance for over a decade. I've visited our programs from Iraq to Jordan, Gaza and the West Bank, to Central African Republic, to Lebanon. And during that time, the number of children affected by conflict has more than doubled, from 230 million in 2014 to more than 520 million today. Every year, more children are killed and maimed in conflict than the year before. In 2025, over 70% of these deaths were from explosive weapons. The United Nations keeps the record. And the record shows that it is state armed forces that are now the primary perpetrators of killing children, of maiming them, of attacking their schools and their hospitals, of blocking the aid meant to reach them. When explosive weapons are used in populated areas, 96% of the casualties are civilians. Too many of these are children. Looking ahead, we cannot ignore the impacts of new technologies in war and the implications for children. Drones have become the weapon of choice. Drone use has risen 4,000% between 2020 and 2024 in Ukraine and the Democratic Republic of Congo across the Central Sahel. Meanwhile, the fast and unregulated use of AI during conflict creates a plethora of new protection risks. I want to tell you the story of one boy. Khaled was eight years old when an Israeli air strike destroyed the house where his family had sought refuge in Gaza. Khaled's mother was killed, his father was killed, his brothers and sisters were killed. Khaled survived. But survival alone is not a satisfactory outcome for the children of our world. The explosion lasts seconds, its consequences last a lifetime. Khaled barely spoke, he isolated himself, he rejected school, but with the appropriate support, he was able to recover. Consistency, education, counseling, play. He began moving and talking, laughing and learning. He returned to childhood. Children's brains are continuously developing. They are built to respond to danger. For that, the brain releases cortisol, adrenaline, the chemistry of survival. Our bodies are designed to deploy these chemicals in a moment of crisis, not for a year, not for the duration of a childhood. When it is released repeatedly, it's toxic. But here's what the evidence also tells us. Healing is possible. And every single child exposed to this violence has the right to this support. Children affected by conflict should be recognized as a global priority, and investment in their mental health and well-being must be considered as important as investment in their physical health and survival. Healing matters, but healing cannot become a substitute for prevention. Compassion matters, but compassion cannot become a substitute for accountability. If we are here to talk about the effects of explosive weapons on children, we have to talk about Gaza. Khaled's story was not inevitable, but the result of a choice to use explosive weapons which, by their nature, can be devastatingly indiscriminate. In Gaza, a quarter of a million tons of explosives have been dropped on one of the most densely populated places in the world, where 50% of the population are children. The UN Independent Commission of Inquiry concluded that the actions of the government of Israel in Gaza meet the threshold of genocide. This is consistent with what children and families are telling us. In Gaza and in conflicts around the globe, we see states and their allies dismiss the rules of law as irrelevant to their interests. We see the guardrails of proportionality expanded to justify the killing of dozens of civilians to hit a single military target. I've seen the long-lasting effects of explosive weapons on children's lives. I've spent time with children recruited by armed groups in Central African Republic, in temporary settlements in Lebanon, with children in refugee camps outside Mosul, at homes in Kibbutz near Oz in Israel, where I saw grenade marks on children's windowsills. I can never get these images out of my head. We must demand accountability. States have obligations under international law to protect children, and states make choices what weapons are used, what weapons are sold, and to whom they are given. Everyone here is a human being that is part of a decision-making chain, and we need to leave here today and scrutinize every single move that we make, because the stakes are simply too high. In fact, I can't think of a higher stake than the life of a child. It is not just our legal obligation to protect children, it is our moral duty. If our societies are made-up by the stories we tell about ourselves, is this really the story we want told about us in this moment? We must not allow ourselves, even for a minute longer, to look away from our own humanity. Thank you.

Thank you. Thank you, Marcus. And thank you to all the panelists for your rich contributions today. And so many, as so many of our distinguished panelists have spoken to this morning, children's lived experience are at the heart of why adherence to the political declaration on strengthening the protection of civilians from the humanitarian consequences arising from the use of explosive weapons in populated areas is so critical. I'd now like you to turn your attention to the screen to hear directly from those children who need our action. Children who should have been in the chamber with us today.

So, the school is not renovated, and the teachers are not happy with the distance learning. much in my mother's team of chat.

It's a school is the boat is not yet. D'abord, vers les avenues du haut de mon quartier, les dégâts que je peux constater ici, c'est affligeant.

أول ذكرى إلي بالحرب كانت يمكن كان عمري ثلاث سنوات فقط فجأة صحيت على صوت انفجار الدجاج متكسر من حولي وأهلنا عم يصرخوا يلا بسرعة يلا بسرعة من وقتها من بعد ما صار شنطة سفر وطريقنا التهجير كل ما نتعود على مكان ونتركه تحت القصف وكل ما نحط صديق نودعه من شنو طريقة تم من بداية الحرب قلنا نطلع من الفاشل فقدت بيتنا فقدت أصحابي

But we have to build a new life because the war has stopped.

And I hope it won't return.

It's sad, but it will be better.

I have a small hope in my heart that there will be a better future, God willing. But we, the people of Goma, we want only one thing, peace and security for us, for our loved ones, our family.

We will now open the floor to hear from member states and civil society. We will invite speakers to take the floor with consideration given to regional distribution and champions of this critical agenda, ensuring diverse perspectives. When taking the floor, speakers should press the microphone button on the table in front of them to activate their microphone before beginning the intervention. And I need to emphasize, given the number of important voices we have in the room today, I will give the floor to each registered speaker for two to three minutes only, and the microphone will be turned off at three minutes. This is to ensure that everyone can speak and we can hear a diverse set of voices. To begin, I'm going to invite the speaker from Andorra to give their statement.

Thank you. Excellencies, distinguished participants, ladies and gentlemen, 30 years ago, the United Nations established the mandate for a Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General on Children and Armed Conflict with a clear purpose, to ensure that children who bear no responsibility for war are protected from its consequences. Three decades later, we are confronted with a deeply troubling reality. The number of children killed and injured in armed conflict continues to rise, and explosive weapons remain one of the leading causes of these casualties, particularly when used in populated areas. Behind every figure, there is a child whose life has been changed forever. Early this year, Andorra had the privilege of welcoming Junior Nsita Ntsuami as part of the Prove It Matters campaign, which Andorra and Malta proudly support. Abducted in the Democratic Republic of Congo at the age of 12 while he was at school, Junior was forced to become a child soldier. Meeting him in Andorra was a powerful reminder that behind the statistics, there are real children whose childhoods have been stolen by war. His story also illustrates a simple truth: children belong in schools, not on battlefields. They should carry books and pens, not weapons. For children, the impact of an explosive attack does not end when the explosion stops. Destroyed schools interrupt education, damaged hospitals limit access to care, destroyed water and sanitation infrastructure threaten children's health and survival. And the long-term psychological impact can last a lifetime. This is why protecting children must begin with prevention. Andorra endorsed the Declaration on Strengthening the Protection of Civilians from the Humanitarian Consequences Arising from the Use of Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas in Dublin in 2022, and remains committed in integrating the protection of children into its multilateral engagement. But endorsement alone is not enough. Political commitments must lead to concrete action. This is also particularly important as warfare evolves. The growing use of drones, autonomous systems.
Thank you to the speaker from Andorra. And I'd like to move to the speaker from Austria.

Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen. The protection of children in armed conflict and addressing the impact of explosive weapons in populated areas have been long-standing priorities for Austria. As we mark the 30th anniversary of the Children and Armed Conflict mandate, its relevance could hardly be clearer given the horrifying scale of violence affecting children. With explosive weapons responsible for almost 70% of child casualties, it is clear that addressing their use must be a central part of our efforts. Austria attaches particular importance to prevention, including full respect for international humanitarian law and protection of schools, hospitals and other civilian infrastructure. The Safe Schools Declaration and the Eviper Declaration are key instruments in this regard. We are also passionate advocates for strengthening accountability for violations, including through the monitoring and reporting mechanism and for an impartial and evidence-based CARC agenda. And the evolving means and methods of warfare through the use of drones and the integration of AI present new challenges. Austria is a strong advocate for addressing the humanitarian consequences of explosive weapons in populated areas. In 2019, we hosted the Vienna Conference on Protecting Civilians in Urban Warfare, which was instrumental in the establishment of the Wiper Declaration. Since then, we have remained actively engaged in its universalization and implementation. The interconnection between these two agendas is clear. The use of explosive weapons in populated areas kills, maims and injures children. It also destroys the infrastructure and support systems on which their lives depend: schools and hospitals, water and sanitation systems, homes and energy infrastructure. Explosive remnants of war often continue to endanger children long after the fighting has stopped. Thirty years after the establishment of the CAC mandate, our task is to turn these normative frameworks into concrete action. The Evipa commitments provide an excellent basis to strengthen military policies and practices, training, data collection, victim assistance, and measures to address both the direct and reverberating effects of explosive weapons. Through the implementation, children will become safer. At the same time, we should also dedicate greater resources to ensuring that children themselves can participate in our work on the CARC agenda, empowering them to become positive actors in society. Thank you.
Thank you to the speaker from Austria. I'd like to invite the speaker from Costa Rica.

Thank you very much. Costa Rica thanks you for convening this meeting on the 30th anniversary of the Mandate on Children and Armed Conflict. For a child, the use of explosive weapons in populated areas can mean losing their home, their school, or access to water and medical care. The consequences endure long after hostilities have ceased. Our response must address both visible and invisible wounds. As a country without an army, Costa Rica maintains that the conduct of hostilities must fully respect international humanitarian law. The principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution require consideration of the foreseeable effects on the services children depend on. In June 2015, we endorsed the Safe Schools Declaration to protect education during armed conflict. We also endorsed the Political Declaration on the Use of Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas and hosted its second international follow-up conference in San Jose. Following that conference, Costa Rica, Ireland and Norway issued an outcome document recommending that states review national policies and practices, improve data collection on indirect effects and strengthen assistance to victims. It is now time to put those recommendations into practice. Excellencies, Technologies transforming conflict pose new challenges. Whatever means are employed, decisions on the use of force must comply with international law. No technology justifies endangering civilian lives, especially those of children. We invite more states to endorse the political declaration and work toward its implementation. Protecting children is a shared responsibility and a condition for building peace. Thank you very much.
Thank you to the speaker from Costa Rica. I'd like to invite the speaker from Belgium.

Excellencies, 30 years after the mandate of the Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflicts was established, we continue to witness an ongoing increase globally of verified grave violations against children, and it is of great concern to my country. This negative trend is the sign of a real and dangerous erosion of respect for and compliance with international humanitarian law and international human rights law. The unique impact of explosive weapons in populated areas on children is undeniable. It is indeed one of the main causes of grave violations against their rights, specifically killing and maiming, but also attacks on schools and hospitals. Belgium reaffirms its commitment to international humanitarian law and the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution. We believe that the implementation of the EU-IPA political declaration must be rooted in this legal obligation, while also going further to promote good practices. Around the world, Belgian diplomatic missions are active as a member of chair or chair of groups of friends related to children and armed conflict agenda. You can count on my country to integrate the declaration's common commitments into the work of these groups and to advocate within and through these groups for the universal adoption of the declaration. I thank you.
Thank you to the speaker from Belgium. I'd like to invite the speaker from Syria.

Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, in Syria, the danger of war doesn't end when the fighting stops. Today, mines and unexploded ordnance are present across the country. Through our work, we have identified nine different types of mines, as Syria is the second most contaminated country in the world. And 30% of those who have been killed by explosive remnants since December 2024 are children. This is why at our Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management, we established the National Mine Action Center, where we are building a national system, consolidating data, identifying contaminated areas, setting national standards, coordinating surveys and clearance, and building Syrian technical capacity. We are also developing a three-year national strategy, because this cannot remain a collection of fragmented projects. For us, national ownership is essential. We need international partners to provide expertise, equipment, and financing, but this support must build sustainable Syria national capacity, not to replace it. Syria must be able to set its own priorities, coordinate actors, manage national data, and direct survey and clearance efforts to areas of the greatest need. Mine action is not separate technical file. It's a precondition for return, restoring of services, reopening school, and bringing agriculture land back into use. This is why getting the sequence right is essential to recovery. Therefore, we adopted area-based approach, linking survey and the clearance priorities directly to areas seeing population return. On the other hand, we also need to ensure sustained support for victims and survivors. 30 years after the establishment of the Children and Armed Conflicts Mandate, we don't need more words. We need compliance. Thank you.
Thank you to the speaker from Syria. I'd like to invite the speaker from Ireland.

Thank you, Madam Moderator, Excellencies and colleagues. I would like to thank everyone who was involved in organising this meeting on what is a very critical issue. I think it reminds us all that we can never become immune to the horrific reality of conflict, particularly conflict affecting children, which children should never have to endure. Since the adoption of the EUWIP political declaration in Dublin in 2022, we continue to work to universalise the declaration, particularly with Norway and Costa Rica, who have hosted recent implementation conferences. The UN Secretary General's report on children in armed conflict highlights the scale of the awful reality. That children are killed or injured in conflict is unconscionable in and of itself, and such deaths are so often the direct result of the use of explosive weapons in populated areas. And as many people have testified, behind the high numbers cited in the Secretary-General's report are real traumas that will have long-lasting impacts for individuals, for families and for communities across generations. That is why Ireland continues to champion the Uweipa declaration and why we continue to engage in outreach to help develop a life-saving norm and change military practices. It is precisely at this time of increased conflict that we should champion the declaration and prioritise universalisation and enhanced implementation on the ground. It is such an important tool for reaffirming and operationalising key obligations under international law. The Wiper Political Declaration makes important commitments that if developed and implemented widely will help to strengthen the protection of civilians, including children. And I think as we've heard from the powerful testimony today, implementation is so important. When reporting on the declaration, set out concrete changes in doctrine, training and practice, including those specifically designed to protect children. Ultimately, the most effective way to protect children from explosive weapons is to avoid their use in populated areas altogether. Thank you.

Thank you. Excellencies, colleagues, as we close, I would like to leave you with five powerful messages from today's side event. First, The scale of harm demands urgent action. Behind each figure is a child, as we heard our Minister say before, Minister Fan.
